summary:
Stephanie Jarmak, a former astronomer with zero commits a year ago and now 12,000 commits maintaining a multi-agent orchestration framework, delivers a talk titled 'The Death of Developer Advocates' on behalf of her vacationing manager. She argues DevRel is not dead, but its audience has shifted in 2026: developers orchestrate fleets of agents, and non-engineers gain shipping capability, expanding the ICP beyond traditional developer personas.

The agent is framed as a dual user. It reads docs, calls APIs, hits errors, and recovers, while also recommending tools to humans via chat assistants or autonomous installs. Jarmak built CodeScaleBench, hundreds of SDLC tasks run with and without Sourcegraph's code navigation MCP tool, producing thousands of traces. In one trace, the model guessed a parameter name ('read line' instead of 'start line'), failed, recovered from the error text, but burned an entire turn, a problem a clearer tool description would have prevented. Buyers now judge tools on tokens and latency, not just correctness.

Her GEO experiment compared shopping-style versus pain-style prompts: shopping prompts surfaced Sourcegraph 65% of the time; pain prompts (e.g., breaking downstream services) produced zero mentions, with the agent suggesting a wiki page. Stale training data compounds, with Sonnet 4 even recommending the deprecated Cody product. Mitigation requires llms.txt-style authoritative pages, real-time provenance, FAQs, charts, presence in MCP registries, and zero-friction adoption paths. DevRel now spans engineering (MCP interfaces, evals), product (agentic experience rubrics), and marketing (GEO funnel) flavors. Core DevRel functions still hold: enablement for both human and machine audiences, community (now with privacy considerations for agent-in-the-loop conversations), feedback loops amplified by running thousands of agent experiments, and credibility, including awareness that agents favor their own content style. Jarmak closes with the curb cut argument: serving agents clears the human path too. Concrete next steps include pointing a coding agent at one's docs and running GEO mention-vs-recommendation experiments.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: An astronomer, an agent advocate, and a borrowed title
sections.summary: Jarmak introduces herself as a former astronomer with zero commits a year ago and now 12,000 commits maintaining a multi-agent orchestration framework. Her manager, a real developer advocate, submitted the provocative talk title and went on vacation, so she delivers his 'eulogy' as the 'agent advocate.' She traces DevRel history from 1980s software evangelism through 2010s advocacy feedback loops to 2026, when developers orchestrate agents and non-engineers gain shipping capability.

sections.title: What changes when developers stop working alone
sections.summary: Developers are no longer working alone; they orchestrate fleets of agents and need AI fluency. Non-engineers like Jarmak can ship OSS via agents, expanding the DevRel ICP beyond traditional developer personas.

sections.title: The agent as a user, and as a recommender
sections.summary: The agent is a dual user: it reads docs, calls APIs, hits errors, and recovers. It also recommends tools to humans via chat assistants or by directly installing libraries in workflows. This shifts DevRel's bottom-up adoption mechanics into the agent layer.

sections.title: Benchmarking agents with and without your tool
sections.summary: Jarmak built CodeScaleBench with hundreds of SDLC tasks, run with and without Sourcegraph's code navigation MCP tool, producing thousands of traces for tight feedback loops. The goal is to see exactly where agent-tool interaction breaks down and to fix it.

sections.title: A whole turn burned on a guessed parameter
sections.summary: In one trace, the model guessed a parameter name like 'read line' instead of 'start line,' failed, recovered from the error text, but burned an entire turn. Buyers now evaluate tools on tokens and latency, so this friction matters and must be measured.

sections.title: Generative engine optimization, and a 65 to zero gap
sections.summary: Jarmak ran a GEO experiment comparing shopping-style vs. pain-style prompts. Shopping prompts produced 65% Sourcegraph recommendations; pain prompts (e.g., breaking downstream services) produced zero, with the agent suggesting a wiki page. The gap is invisible without measurement, prompting a content campaign with measurable lift.

sections.title: Why stale content compounds against you
sections.summary: Training data is always stale and compounds old product references. Sonnet 4 recommended the deprecated Cody product, and a rerun with 4.6 made it worse. Solutions include keeping content fresh with current examples, llms.txt-style authoritative pages, FAQs, charts, and giving the agent quotable material with real-time provenance.

sections.title: Be where the agents are, and cut the friction
sections.summary: Make sure the product is in MCP registries and agent marketplaces wherever an agent would look. Reduce the friction from discovery to embedding: if adoption requires multiple demos or sales-rep emails, an agent will not surface the tool. Also ensure enough pain-style content exists on the open web for agents to recognize and connect real use cases to the product.

sections.title: What still holds: enablement, community, feedback, and credibility
sections.summary: DevRel now spans engineering (MCP interfaces, evals, instrumentation), product (end-to-end agentic experience rubrics), and marketing (GEO funnel ownership) flavors that can be mixed and matched. Core DevRel still holds: enablement for humans and machines, community (with new privacy considerations for agent-in-the-loop conversations), feedback loops amplified by running thousands of agent experiments, and credibility, including the asymmetric finding that agents favor their own content style.

sections.title: The curb cut argument and concrete next steps
sections.summary: Jarmak closes with the curb cut analogy: ramps built for wheelchairs now benefit strollers, suitcases, and any wheeled user. By serving agents, the human path gets cleared too. Concrete next steps: point a coding agent at one's own docs and build an agent experience report, or start a GEO mention-vs-recommendation experiment. The talk itself is made agent-legible via a QR code and template toy repos.

demonstrations: CodeScaleBench: hundreds of SDLC tasks run with and without Sourcegraph's code navigation MCP, producing thousands of traces.
Trace example: agent guessed parameter 'read line' instead of 'start line', failed, recovered from error, burned one full turn.
GEO prompt experiment: shopping-style vs. pain-style prompts returning 65% vs. 0% Sourcegraph recommendation rate.

limitations: Training data is always stale and compounding old product references (e.g., Cody) bury current signal.
Pain-style prompts surfaced zero mentions, indicating messaging fails to attribute real use cases clearly to agents.
If a tool requires multiple demos or sales-rep emails, agents will not recommend it to users.
Agents exhibit self-preference bias toward their own content style (e.g., tolerating m dashes), creating asymmetric credibility landscapes for humans vs. agents.
Bringing agents into community spaces (e.g., Discord) introduces new privacy and data-recording concerns.
